title: (C.) THE SNAKE DANCE (Illustration)
note: Marked "(C.)" before the subject in the catalogue: in competition for the Clarke prize (catalogue Memoranda, PDF p. 26). Catalogue text: “The Snake Dance” is a solemn bi-annual ceremony of the Moqui Indians of Arizona. It is the culminating rite in a series of ceremonies, and is the most remarkable survival of prehistoric nature worship extant. It is probably a petition for rain. The dance occurs at sunset in a plaza in the pueblo of Wal-pi, about seven hundred feet above the surrounding plain. The snake priests are the active participants; their bodies are stained with red and their faces are with black—the streamers of red buckskin typifying the snakes. The priests are divided into groups of three, the “Carrier,” who places one or more of the snakes between his lips when he is supposed to become at once blind; the “Hugger,” who supports him, endeavors with his whip to attract the snakes' attention, and the “Gatherer,” who walks behind and secures the snakes that may be dropped. At the end of the dance the snakes are liberated to bear the petitions to the Gods. Dimensions as printed in the catalogue's illustration caption: 84 x 144.
